entry: British singer-songwriter and musician. He has sold more than 100 million records. Stevens released albums including *Tea for the Tillerman* (1970) and *Teaser and the Firecat* (1971), both certified triple platinum in the U.S. He converted to Islam in December 1977, adopted the name Yusuf Islam the following year, and auctioned his guitars for charity in 1979 before largely leaving secular music. He returned to pop with *An Other Cup* (2006) and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2014. In 1989 his comments about the fatwa against [[Salman Rushdie]] drew controversy; he stated that he never supported the fatwa.

Western Romance language native to the eastern Iberian Peninsula. It shares official status with Spanish in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and the Valencian Community, where it is called Valencian, and is the sole official language of [[Andorra]]. It evolved from Vulgar Latin in the [[Middle Ages]] and was the language of the Principality of Catalonia and the kingdoms of Valencia and Mallorca. Spanish replaced it in government and literature in the 1700s. A literary revival in 19th-century Spain culminated in the early 1900s. Under the Francoist dictatorship (1936–1975) its use was repressed, and it was renormalized between the 1980s and 2000s.

Autonomous community in northeastern Spain, designated a nationality by its Statute of Autonomy. Its capital and largest city is [[Barcelona]], and with a population of 8,124,126 it is the second-most populous autonomous community in Spain. Catalonia's history includes a 1137 dynastic union between the County of Barcelona and the [[Kingdom of Aragon]] and, after Barcelona's capitulation in 1714, the suppression of its institutions. Self-government was restored in 1975–1982. Growing support for independence followed, and the Catalan Parliament declared independence on 27 October 2017 after a referendum that was deemed unconstitutional. Spain then imposed direct rule. Those imprisoned were pardoned in 2021. Polls have indicated persistent but minority support for secession.

Exhaust emission control device. It converts toxic gases from an [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]] into less-toxic pollutants by catalyzing a [[Redox|redox reaction]]. To comply with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency rules, most gasoline-powered vehicles from the 1975 model year were equipped with catalytic converters. Three-way converters, which also reduce oxides of nitrogen (NOx), were first commercialized by Volvo on 1977 cars. Almost all automakers adopted them for the 1981 model year. Catalysts are coated with precious metals, typically [[Platinum]], palladium and rhodium.

Ballistic device that launches projectiles using stored potential energy, without gunpowder or other propellants. Most catapults release tension or torsion that was built up slowly by hand, using springs, bows or twisted rope. Ancient and medieval catapults were siege engines, and in ancient times were usually the strongest heavy weaponry. The earliest date to at least the 7th century BC, when King Uzziah of Judah equipped the walls of Jerusalem with machines that shot "great stones." Greek catapults were used at the siege of Motya in 397 BC. The mangonel appeared in ancient China in the 5th century BC. Modern devices include the hand-held slingshot and aircraft launchers on ships.

Neuropsychiatric syndrome marked by abnormal movement and behavior. It is most commonly seen in people with mood disorders such as [[Major depressive disorder|major depressive disorder]] or psychotic disorders such as [[Schizophrenia]]. Affected people may be withdrawn and nearly motionless for days, or perform repetitive, purposeless movements. Subtypes include stuporous, excited, malignant and periodic catatonia. Treatment with [[Benzodiazepine|benzodiazepines]] or electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the most effective and leads to remission of symptoms in most cases.

Satirical war novel by Joseph Heller, first published in 1961. It is set during World War II and follows Captain John Yossarian, a U.S. Army Air Forces bombardier who tries to avoid further combat missions. The novel satirizes military bureaucracy and greed through a non-chronological narrative. The title refers to a rule under which a pilot deemed insane could be grounded, but any request for grounding on grounds of insanity showed sufficient rationality to keep flying. The phrase has entered English to mean a no-win situation. A 1970 film, directed by Mike Nichols, was followed by a 2019 miniseries produced by George Clooney.

Australian actor and producer. She made her feature film debut in 1997 and came to international prominence as Queen Elizabeth I in *Elizabeth* (1998). She won [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for *The Aviator* (2004) and *Blue Jasmine* (2013), and has been the most-nominated Australian. Blanchett has performed in more than twenty stage productions. She and her husband, Andrew Upton, were artistic directors of the Sydney Theatre Company from 2008 to 2013. She has received several honorary awards, including the Companion of the Order of Australia in 2017.

General theory of mathematical structures and their relations. It was introduced by Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane in the mid-20th century in their foundational work on [[Algebraic topology|algebraic topology]], and it can be used in most areas of mathematics. A category consists of objects and morphisms (arrows) that compose, which must satisfy associativity and identity. A functor maps between categories, and a natural transformation relates functors. Many constructions, such as quotient spaces and direct products, are unified in its terms. Many areas of [[Computer science|computer science]], such as [[Functional programming|functional programming]] and semantics, also rely on it.

Order of ray-finned fish, Siluriformes, named for prominent barbels that resemble a cat's whiskers, though not all catfish have them. Catfish have no [[Scale (zoology)|scales]], and their skin is smooth or armoured. The order includes about 3,400 valid species in 37 families, mostly freshwater. The largest species include the Mekong giant catfish of [[Southeast Asia]], the wels catfish of Eurasia and the piraíba of South America, while the tiny candiru is an ectoparasite. Many catfish are farmed or fished for food. Smaller species such as *Corydoras* are important in the [[Aquarium|aquarium]] hobby, and some plecos have become invasive through it.

French actress. A major figure of the New Wave, she has played more than a hundred roles in a career spanning nearly 70 years, including *The Umbrellas of Cherbourg* (1964) and *Belle de Jour* (1967). Her films have attracted nearly 99 million spectators in French theaters, the most admissions of any working actress in France. In 1985 she succeeded Mireille Mathieu as the official face of Marianne, France's national symbol of liberty. In 2018 she co-signed a *Le Monde* open letter criticizing what its authors called puritanical excesses of the [[MeToo movement]]. The letter drew both support and backlash.

Welsh actress. She won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as Velma Kelly in *Chicago* (2002). She won a Tony Award for Best Actress in a Musical for her role in the Broadway production of *A Little Night Music* (2009). Her other films include *Traffic* (2000), *Ocean's Twelve* (2004) and *The Terminal* (2004). She was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2010 for her film and humanitarian work. She has been open about her experience with [[Bipolar II disorder|bipolar II disorder]]. She is married to actor [[Michael Douglas]].

Queen consort of France (1547–59) and regent for her sons. Born in Florence to Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, she was orphaned within weeks of her birth. In 1533, at age 14, she married the future Henry II, son of [[Francis I of France|Francis I]]. Henry largely excluded her from state affairs, and she came into power after his death in 1559 as mother of Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III. Her sons reigned amid the [[French Wars of Religion]]. She first made concessions to the [[Huguenots]] and later adopted hardline policies against them. She was blamed for the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, in which thousands of Huguenots were killed. Some historians excuse her from blame for the worst decisions of the crown, while her letters are cited as evidence of ruthlessness. She also patronized the arts, commissioning the Tuileries Palace and fostering court ballet. Her patronage is part of the [[Renaissance]] in France.

Queen of England (1509–33) as the first wife of [[Henry VIII]]. The youngest child of [[Isabella I of Castile|Isabella I of Castile]] and [[Ferdinand II of Aragon|Ferdinand II of Aragon]], she was first married to Henry's elder brother Arthur, who died five months after their 1501 wedding. She served as regent of England in 1513 while Henry was in France. When Henry sought an annulment to marry Anne Boleyn, Catherine refused to accept it or his supremacy over the Church in England. She died in banishment at Kimbolton Castle. Her daughter [[Mary I]] became the first undisputed English queen regnant in 1553.

Vacuum tube with one or more electron guns that display images on a phosphorescent screen. The images may represent waveforms on an [[Oscilloscope|oscilloscope]], television frames, computer-monitor graphics or radar targets. Electron beams are steered by deflection coils or plates. Color tubes control three beams, one for each primary color. The interior is evacuated to less than a millionth of atmospheric pressure, and the thick face is made of lead or barium-strontium glass to block X-rays. J. J. Thomson showed in 1897 that cathode rays were negatively charged particles, the first subatomic particles identified. Since the late 2000s CRTs have been superseded by flat-panel displays such as [[Liquid-crystal display|liquid-crystal displays]], plasma and OLED, which are lighter and thinner.

Concept of beliefs and practices widely accepted by Christian denominations that describe themselves as catholic. The term derives from the Greek *katholikos*, meaning "general" or "universal." The [[Nicene Creed]] calls the Church "one, holy, catholic, and apostolic." Catholicity refers to the full wholeness of the Christian faith, proclaimed to all people without excluding any part. The 5th-century Vincentian Canon defined catholic belief as "what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all." The trait is ascribed to the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] and other churches, and is used by Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed denominations to claim continuity with the apostolic faith. The capitalized Catholic usually refers to the [[Catholic Church]].

Roman soldier, senator and historian, known for his conservatism and opposition to Hellenization. Also called Cato the Censor, he was elected consul in 195 BC and censor in 184 BC. As censor he introduced taxes on luxuries and oversaw extensive public works. His attacks forced [[Scipio Africanus]] into retirement. He wrote the *Origines*, the first history of Rome written in Latin, and *De agri cultura*, a treatise on agriculture that is the oldest extant prose in Latin. Late in life he became a vigorous opponent of [[Carthage]], reportedly ending speeches with *Carthago delenda est* ("Carthage must be destroyed"). His epithet Elder distinguishes him from his great-grandson Cato the Younger.

Sung-through musical with music by [[Andrew Lloyd Webber|Andrew Lloyd Webber]], based on T. S. Eliot's poetry collection *Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats* (1939). It follows the Jellicles, a tribe of cats who choose one member to ascend to the Heaviside Layer and be reborn. The show opened in the [[London|West End]] in 1981 and on Broadway in 1982. The London production ran for 21 years and 8,949 performances, and the Broadway production for 18 years and 7,485 performances. It started the megamusical phenomenon, and its worldwide gross reached US$3.5 billion by 2012. A 2019 film was directed by Tom Hooper.

Roman poet of the late [[Roman Republic|Roman Republic]], born in Verona to a leading equestrian family. He was a leading figure among the *neoteroi*, or "new poets," who wrote concise, personal lyrics. His 116 surviving short poems include erotic verse, satirical lampoons and hymns. About 25 poems address "Lesbia," usually identified as Clodia Metelli, tracing an affair through euphoria, doubts, separation and loss. He spent 57–56 BC in Bithynia on the staff of Gaius Memmius. Suetonius reports that [[Julius Caesar|Julius Caesar]], whom Catullus had lampooned, invited him to dinner on the day he apologized. His poems influenced later Augustan poets.

Ancient state in the Caucasus, mostly overlapping present-day [[Azerbaijan]]. The name Albania derives from Greek sources that incorrectly translated the Armenian language, and the prefix "Caucasian" distinguishes it from the Balkan Albania. In 252 it acknowledged the suzerainty of the [[Sasanian Empire]], and it remained part of that empire until its fall. Its kings were replaced by an Arsacid family by the end of the 3rd century, and by the Mihranids in the 5th century. Its population spoke Northeast Caucasian languages, unrelated to Indo-European Albanian. The kingdom adopted Christianity as state religion in the early 4th century.

Mountain range at the intersection of Asia and Europe, stretching between the [[Black Sea]] and the [[Caspian Sea]]. It comprises the Greater Caucasus in the north and the Lesser Caucasus in the south, which are connected by the Likhi Range. [[Mount Elbrus]], at 5,642 m (18,510 ft), is the highest peak in Europe. The Greater Caucasus was folded largely by the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian plates. The region is seismically active, and the 1988 Spitak earthquake destroyed the Gyumri–Vanadzor region of Armenia. The Caucasus Mountains were part of the [[Silk Road]].

Geographical region spanning Eastern Europe and Western Asia, between the [[Black Sea]] and the [[Caspian Sea]]. It comprises parts of southern [[Russia]], [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], [[Armenia]] and [[Azerbaijan]], and is divided into the North Caucasus and the South Caucasus. The [[Caucasus Mountains]] have conventionally been seen as a natural barrier between Europe and Asia. The region is linguistically diverse, with Kartvelian, Northwest Caucasian and Northeast Caucasian families indigenous alongside Indo-European and Turkic languages. According to Pliny the Elder's *Natural History*, the name derives from a Scythian term meaning "shimmering with snow."

Mathematical inequality bounding the inner product of two vectors. In an [[Inner product space|inner product space]], the absolute value of the inner product is at most the product of the vectors' [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]], with equality if and only if the vectors are linearly dependent. Augustin-Louis Cauchy published the inequality for sums in 1821. Viktor Bunyakovsky published the integral version in 1859 and Hermann Schwarz in 1888, and Schwarz gave the modern proof. It is considered one of the most important and widely used inequalities in mathematics.

Theorem in [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]] giving integral formulas for all derivatives of a [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic function]]. It states that a holomorphic function defined on a disk is completely determined by its values on the disk's boundary. For an interior point a, f(a) = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − a) dz, where the contour is the circle bounding the disk, oriented counterclockwise. Consequently, holomorphic functions are analytic and infinitely differentiable. The theorem is named after [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy|Augustin-Louis Cauchy]], and it extends to any closed rectifiable curve with winding number one about the point.

Vegetable of the species *Brassica oleracea*, grown for its dense head of undeveloped flower buds, known as the curd. It belongs to the [[Brassicaceae|cabbage family]], along with [[Broccoli]], [[Cabbage]], Brussels sprouts and kale. Cauliflower was domesticated in the Mediterranean region during antiquity, most likely by [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]] of wild cabbage. The head is usually white, but cultivars may be green, orange or purple. The Romanesco variety has spiral curds that grow in [[Fractal|fractal]] patterns. Production of cauliflower combined with broccoli was 27 million tonnes in 2024, led by [[China]] and [[India]] with 73% of the total.
